### Category

Projects/Platforms/Tools/Services

### Resource Name

VibeKit.bot

### URL

https://vibekit.bot

### Description

VibeKit gives every app its own persistent AI coding agent that builds it, hosts it on a live domain, and keeps improving it, driven from your phone or the CLI. Unlike one-shot generators, the agent keeps working after the first prototype: no laptop to keep awake, and it survives a dropped connection. BYOK for Claude/OpenAI or pay-as-you-go, with a free tier.

### Additional Context

Suggested entry for `Cloud & Platform Integrations` (peers: Replit, Bolt.new, Lovable, Emergent, Playcode):

```md
| [**VibeKit.bot**](https://vibekit.bot) | Persistent AI coding agent per app that builds, hosts (live domain), and keeps improving it, driven from your phone or CLI; BYOK or pay-as-you-go |
```

Why it fits: none of the current entries cover driving the whole build/host/improve loop from a phone via a persistent hosted agent (there is also a native iOS app: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/vibekit-agent-devops/id6760206636).

Disclosure: I'm the maker. Naming note: "VibeKit.bot" disambiguates us from the unrelated, discontinued npm SDK "vibekit" (superagent-ai/vibekit); we're the hosted app builder at vibekit.bot.

title: Tracking: Master implementation order and dependency graph
content:
> **How to use this:** Start at Step 1. Finish it before moving to Step 2. Within each step, issues marked ↕ can be picked in any order — choose whichever interests you most.

---

## 👉 Step 1 — Quick bug fixes *(start today, no setup needed)*

These are self-contained fixes. None of them depend on anything else. Pick one, fix it, open a PR, move to the next.

| # | What to fix | Why it matters | Effort | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **#12A** | Add button in the resource panel throws a `ReferenceError` on every click — one missing import line | Broken feature — users can't add resources | ~5 min | ✅ Done — merged PR #29 |
| **#2** | Four checklist bugs: stale toggle closure (2–4 clicks to uncheck), Firebase echo race, stale snapshot in filter/phase handlers, phase progress counter lag | Checklist unusable without these fixes | ~2 hr total | ✅ Done — merged PR #31 |
| **#23** | After sign-out, the previous user's roadmap is still in `localStorage` — next visitor on the same device sees it | Privacy bug on shared devices | ~30 min | ✅ Done — merged PR #32 |
| **#22** | Three XSS issues: raw `innerHTML` in `dashboard.js`, dangerous `html` key in `el()`, resource URLs not re-validated before rendering as `href` | Security hardening | ~1–2 hr | ✅ Done — merged PR #33 |
| **#27** | `themeToggle.js` registers a subscriber on every page navigation but never removes it — memory grows indefinitely. Also fixes the static `aria-label`. | Memory leak + accessibility | ~1 hr | ✅ Done — merged PR #34 |

**✅ Step 1 complete.** All five bug fixes shipped. → Move to Step 2.

---

## 👉 Step 2 — CI pipeline + test framework *(do these together — they are the gate for all future PRs)*

> ✅ **#30 done — PR #38 merged** — ESLint, Vitest (17 tests), GitHub Actions CI, and branch protection on `main` are all implemented. E2E (Playwright + Firebase Emulator) is tracked in **#37**.

| # | What to do | Effort | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#30** | Set up GitHub Actions PR quality gate: ESLint + Vitest unit/integration tests + Playwright E2E + secret scan + branch protection rules | Large (2–3 days) | ✅ Done — merged PR #38 |
| **#37** | Wire Firebase Emulator into E2E CI and make `test-e2e` a required branch protection check | Medium | ✅ Done — merged PR #40 |
| **#3** | Set up enterprise testing standards, folder structure, coverage requirements, and AI-agent coding rules | Large (2–3 days) | ✅ Done — merged PR #41 |
| **#43** | Living architecture/onboarding doc (Build Log), enterprise issue templates, PR template upgrade, and automated doc-sync enforcement in CI + `.claude/rules/` | Medium (1–2 days) | ✅ Done — merged PR #45 |

> Work #37 and #3 together — #37 completes the E2E leg of the CI pipeline; #3 fills it with comprehensive test coverage. Once both are merged, every future PR is fully checked. **#43 ✅** is safe to run in parallel with #3 (no shared files) and should land before Step 3 so all future PRs/issues use the new templates and enforcement from the start.

**✅ Done with Step 2?** → All future PRs now require passing tests. Move to Step 3.

---

## 👉 Step 3 — Get the app live *(do this early — gives you a real URL to test against)*

Set up Firebase Hosting so every PR gets an automatic preview URL and every merge to `main` auto-deploys. Do #25 and #28 together — they both touch `firebase.json`.

| # | What to do | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **#25 + #28** | Create `firebase.json` with security headers + set up GitHub Actions for auto-deploy | ✅ Done — merged PR #46 (#25) + PR #47 (#28) |

**✅ Done with Step 3?** → You now have a live URL. Move to Step 4.

---

## 👉 Step 4 — Auth improvements *(do these in order within this step)*

| Order | # | What to do | Blocked until | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st | **#13** | Add "Forgot password?" flow with Firebase email link | Step 2 done | ✅ Done — merged PR #48 |
| 2nd | **#14** | Add email verification on sign-up + session persistence + account deletion | #13 done | ✅ Done — merged PR #49 |
| 2nd | **#26** | Improve auth forms: confirm password, strength meter, show/hide toggle, guest option on sign-up | #13 done | ✅ Done — merged PR #50 |

> #14 and #26 both need #13 first, but can be done in parallel with each other.

**✅ Done with Step 4?** → Move to Step 5.

---

## 👉 Step 5 — Core architecture *(these are all independent — pick any order)*

| # | What to do | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **#7** | Rename the product to Ascent — brand system, logo, localStorage key migration | ✅ Done — merged PR #55 |

# KDS Mission Control — Single Communication Thread

## Purpose

This issue is the single durable communication hub for Codex ↔ ChatGPT ↔ CEO coordination.

CEO is currently dealing with too many runtime chats, repeated GitHub execution request chats, side-channel instructions, and project-specific threads. That is creating confusion and wasted quota.

From now on, this issue is the **mission control thread**.

## Core rule

Runtime chats are disposable. GitHub issue threads are durable.

Codex must treat this issue as the primary communication hub unless a specific project issue is explicitly designated as active.

## Operating model

1. CEO can talk to Codex in one new Codex communication chat.
2. Codex must mirror durable status and decisions into this GitHub issue.
3. ChatGPT will read this GitHub issue when CEO asks for CEO Briefs.
4. Project-specific issues remain source documents, but this issue becomes the index and traffic controller.

## Active issue index

### Hlaðvarp / Mission Alpha

- #4 — Mission Alpha launch gates / hardening
- #5 — Subscription entrypoint discovery
- #6 — Revenue Gate MVP by 2026-08-01
- #7 — Previous KDS protocol / reporting / wake bridge rules
- #8 — Hlaðvarp education and expert Q&A discovery

### Health Platform / SecureVault architecture

- hallurg/health-platform-architecture#76 — Case-scoped voice updates stored directly in SecureVault
- hallurg/health-platform-architecture#77 — Emergency flag and 112 escalation guardrails

### Upplýsingaskjár / Home-dashboard

The information-screen project is currently in incident/controlled recovery mode. Its repo is not visible to ChatGPT through the current GitHub connector, so Codex must mirror essential incident status into this Mission Control issue until a durable project issue/repo thread is available.

Current known constraints:

- no clean local git baseline reported
- production responds, but visible screen did not change as expected
- prior unsafe deploy/revert attempts occurred
- admin simplification was implemented locally but not safely deployed
- recovery and deployment require CEO approval after readiness/comparison report

## Codex session rule

At the start of every new Codex runtime session:

1. Read this issue first.
2. Read the latest relevant project issue(s).
3. Post:

```md
## CODEX SESSION CONTINUITY

A. New runtime session started
B. Issues read
C. Active project
D. Current state
E. Next intended action
F. Waiting for approval: yes/no
```

Do not begin implementation before this if there is any ambiguity.

## Stray chat rule

If CEO sends an instruction in a private/runtime chat that is not mirrored in this issue or the relevant project issue, Codex must treat it as draft context only.

Codex must not implement, deploy, restore, or modify production based only on a stray chat instruction.

Required behavior:

1. Stop before action.
2. Summarize the instruction.
3. Post proposed action here or in the relevant project issue.
4. Wait for explicit CEO approval.

## Hourly monitoring rule

Hourly GitHub checks must not create new visible runtime chats/tasks unless there is actionable work, a blocker, or a report.

If no change:

- no-op silently, or
- update one existing status if supported

Do not create a stack of duplicated “GitHub execution request...” chats.

## Reporting markers

Use these markers so ChatGPT can find reports:

```md
## CODEX ENGINEERING REPORT
## CODEX INCIDENT REPORT
## CODEX STRAY SESSION INCIDENT REPORT
## CODEX CLEANUP REPORT
## CODEX DEPLOY READINESS REPORT
## CODEX SESSION CONTINUITY
```

## Approval model

Codex may inspect, read, compare, screenshot, and report without additional approval unless project-specific safety rules say otherwise.

Codex must not do any of the following without explicit CEO approval:

- deploy
- restore
- delete
- rsync
- docker compose up/build/restart in production
- touch `.env`

title: [Feature]: WIP limit / pull system (max concurrent tasks per step or agent)
content:
### Problem

As a user running multiple agents against rate-limited providers, I can't safely stack
work in Backlog — dumping several tasks into an auto-start step (e.g. a "Clarify-AI" gate)
starts one agent session per task in parallel, and the provider starts rejecting requests
(429s / thrashing). I have to manually drip-feed tasks one at a time and babysit the board
instead of trusting kandev to pace the work. There's no way today to cap how many tasks a
given agent/step works on at once on a kanban board, so the throughput I can safely use is
bottlenecked by my own attention, not by kandev.

Verified against current source:

| Mechanism | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Step WIP limits on `WorkflowStep` | **Does not exist** — no limit field on step model. |
| Step events (`on_enter`/`on_exit`) | Only act on the task that fired them — a step's `on_exit` can't pull a *different* task out of queue column, so pull system can't be expressed in workflow YAML alone. |
| `agent_profiles.max_concurrent_sessions` | Column exists (default 1) but **only enforced by Office mode** — kanban orchestrator/lifecycle never reads it, silently ignored on kanban boards. |
| Internal orchestrator queue/scheduler | Priority heap + drain loop exists, but no per-step or per-profile cap user-configurable for this. |

### Proposed solution

Classic Kanban **WIP limit + pull system** on a step:

> At most **N** tasks occupy a given step (or set of steps sharing one agent profile).
> When occupant moves on, slot frees, next task in feeder column (ordered by
> position/priority) pulled in automatically.

Suggested shape:

1. **Schema:** `workflow_steps.wip_limit INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` (0 = unlimited) +
   `pull_from_step_id TEXT` (which column feeds this one).
2. **Model:** expose on `WorkflowStep`/`StepDefinition`, DTO, YAML import/export.
3. **Enforcement (pull side):** on any transition vacating step with `wip_limit > 0`,
   engine (callback alongside existing auto-start/plan-mode callbacks) selects top task
   of `pull_from_step_id`, enqueues move into vacated step, reusing normal move path so
   `on_enter`/auto-start fire normally.
4. **Enforcement (push side, optional):** reject/defer manual and automated moves into
   full step; show `2/1`-style indicator on column header.

### Affected area

Agent lifecycle

### Who needs this?

Not sure

### Target workflow

Fits in the kanban orchestration/workflow engine, not Office mode:

- **Workflow step model** (`internal/workflow/models/models.go`) — `WorkflowStep` gains
  `wip_limit` + `pull_from_step_id`.
- **Callback registry** — new pull-on-exit callback next to existing auto-start /
  plan-mode callbacks, fires on step-vacate transitions.
- **Agent profile** — `agent_profiles.max_concurrent_sessions` is the related cap that
  should extend to kanban, not just Office mode (see Alternatives/Related below).
- **MCP API** — no new surface required; `move_task` already reused by the pull callback,
  so external tooling (dispatchers, automations) keeps working unmodified.
- **UI** — workflow step editor gains WIP limit field + feeder-step picker; board column
  header gains `occupied/limit` indicator.

### Alternatives considered

**Workaround in use today:** external dispatcher (systemd user timer, ~90s tick) polling
MCP API (`list_workflow_steps`, `list_tasks`, `move_task`) — counts occupants of a step,
pulls next queue-column task when a slot frees. Works, deterministic, no LLM involved, but:
- Duplicates logic that belongs in the engine.
- Can't push back on manual drags that exceed the limit (no push-side enforcement).
- External polling adds latency (up to one tick) and an extra moving part per deployment.

**Kandev scheduled automation as dispatcher:** point a `scheduled` (cron) automation with
`execution_mode: run` at a cheap/local agent profile, prompt it to check occupancy and
call `move_task`. Rejected as primary design — non-deterministic, spins up an executor per
tick, a bad parse can move the wrong task. Pure mechanics don't need an LLM in the loop.

**Rely on `agent_profiles.max_concurrent_sessions` alone:** already exists and is exactly
this cap conceptually, but is Office-mode-only; kanban orchestrator never reads it. Could
be the enforcement point instead of a per-step field, but a step-scoped `wip_limit` is more
flexible (lets different steps sharing one profile have independent limits, and covers
workflows that don't use profiles at all). Worth fixing the Office/kanban gap regardless.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `WorkflowStep` supports a configurable `wip_limit` (0/unset = unlimited) via schema,
      model, DTO, and YAML import/export.
- [ ] A step can declare which step feeds it (`pull_from_step_id`).
- [ ] When a step at its `wip_limit` loses an occupant (task transitions out), the top task
      (by position, then priority) in its feeder step is automatically moved in, and normal
      `on_enter`/auto-start behavior fires for that move.
- [ ] Manual/automated moves into a full step are rejected or deferred (push-side), with a
      visible `occupied/limit` indicator on the column header.
- [ ] Behavior is per-workflow: each workflow configures its own steps/limits independently.
- [ ] `agent_profiles.max_concurrent_sessions` enforcement gap on kanban boards is tracked
      (fixed here or as a follow-up issue) so the two mechanisms don't silently conflict.

### Risks and constraints

- **Ordering semantics:** must decide pull order (`position` vs `priority_rank` vs
  `created_at`) — should probably be configurable, not hardcoded.
- **Race conditions:** pull-on-exit and manual drag-in racing on the same slot need a
  single authoritative enforcement point (likely the move path itself) to avoid
  over-filling a step.
- **Long-held slots:** a task can sit in a gate step indefinitely (e.g. waiting on human
  plan approval) — this is correct WIP-limit behavior but should be visible in the UI so
  it doesn't look like a stuck system.
- **Backward compatibility:** default `wip_limit = 0` (unlimited) must keep all existing
  workflows behaving exactly as today — no implicit caps introduced.
- **Scope creep risk:** push-side enforcement (rejecting moves) is more invasive (touches
  manual drag UX, automations, MCP `move_task` callers) than pull-side — may warrant
  splitting into two PRs/issues.

### References

Reference implementation of the pull-side mechanics (external dispatcher, config format,
step/profile mapping) available on request — happy to share the script and paste it into
this issue as a concrete spec if useful, and to send a PR if this design direction is
acceptable.

### Before submitting

- [x] I checked existing issues and did not find this request already tracked.
- [x] This request describes user value, not only an implementation detail.

title: Explore an MCP server for QCobro
content:
## Summary
Investigate exposing QCobro's capabilities via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server so AI agents/tools can interact with the platform programmatically.

## Problem / Motivation
QCobro already has a solid, well-typed API (tRPC over `mods/apiserver`, contracts shared via `mods/common`). As AI agents (including coding/ops agents) and external tooling increasingly rely on MCP as the standard way to interact with services, QCobro currently has no MCP surface — any agent-driven workflow (querying campaigns, contacts, payment promises, gestiones, or triggering outreach) requires bespoke integration instead of a discoverable, standard interface.

## Proposed Solution
Explore wrapping/exposing existing tRPC procedures as MCP tools/resources. Key open questions to research:
- **Architecture**: where the MCP server would live (new `mods/mcp` package vs. a thin layer in `mods/apiserver`) and how it reuses `mods/common` schemas/types rather than duplicating contracts.
- **Auth model**: introduce a dedicated, limited-permission role/scope (via Fonoster Identity) for MCP access, distinct from full operator permissions, so agent-driven actions are scoped down by default (e.g. read-only or a narrow allowlist of mutations).
- **Scope of exposed operations**: which are safe to expose first (read-heavy: contacts, campaigns, payment promises, gestiones) vs. which are too risky for unsupervised agent-initiated writes (e.g. dispatching outreach, marking payments paid).
- **Auditability**: rate limiting and audit logging for MCP-originated actions, since they may be less supervised than operator UI actions.
- **Multi-tenancy**: whether this is a single general MCP server or workspace-scoped, given QCobro's multi-tenant model.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Written exploration/design doc covering rationale, proposed scope, and auth model for an MCP server
- [ ] Recommendation on architecture (where it lives, how it reuses the existing API/schemas)
- [ ] Recommendation on a limited-permission MCP role and which operations it can access
- [ ] Decision on whether/how to proceed (follow-up OpenSpec proposal if approved)

## Priority
P3

title: [BOUNTY] RCS Support [14999$]
content:
**Feature Description:**
Google Messages is currently the only widely available RCS client for Android. When attempting to use Google Messages with microG, users typically encounter issues such as:

A persistent message stating "RCS chats aren't available for this device."
An indefinite "Setting up...", where authentication of the phone number never completes.

Recent developments suggest that Google Messages no longer strictly requires device attestation for RCS, making it possible to enable RCS functionality with microG. However, it appears there's a missing component or necessary adjustment within microG itself preventing successful setup.

Google has effectively monopolized RCS, despite it being a GSMA-backed standard intended as a successor to SMS. Unlike SMS, RCS has become a closed ecosystem under Google's control, restricting open interoperability and limiting choice for users and developers. RCS has seen significant adoption, particularly in North America, and recently Apple added support RCS, further increasing its importance as a messaging standard.

**Requested Solution**

Provide a solution that enables Google Messages to successfully connect to and use RCS functionality when operating with microG. Acceptable outcomes include:
- A fix or enhancement to microG itself, allowing seamless RCS connectivity.
- Compatibility with recent versions of Google Messages is desired. Solutions that only support a specific Google Messages version from the past year will be awarded half of the bounty amount.
- Modifications to AOSP or additional permissions changes are acceptable.
- The solution must work on devices with a locked bootloader.

Limitations
Solutions relying on rooting, Magisk, or similar root-based tools are not acceptable.

**Additional Information**

GrapheneOS users, who leverage a Play services sandbox, have reported success with enabling RCS by applying permission changes. Although their setup differs from microG, the discussions that were taken in this thread (especially in the last year) may offer valuable insights for this bounty: https://discuss.grapheneos.org/d/1353-using-rcs-with-google-messages-on-grapheneos

title: post-training: tool-weighted Gemma 4 E2B v2, four-way continuous eval, and GGUF
content:
## Context

The first Gemma 4 E2B QLoRA pilot trained cleanly but regressed TinyTalk's frozen Linux
strict/static suite from 40% to 36%. The corpus under-represents the operational tools used in
real prompts and does not yet provide a stable four-way continuous comparison or a local GGUF
artifact.

## Scope

- Build a reviewed, license-tracked v2 corpus weighted toward network diagnostics/probing
  (`mtr`, `nmap`, `curl`, `dig`, `ss`, `tcpdump`), Kubernetes, Docker/Compose, RabbitMQ,
  MongoDB, Redis, Kafka, Git, P4, Node, and Python.
- Include safe-use boundaries, destructive/privileged confirmation examples, exact JSON-format
  repair rows, and hard negatives derived from v1 failures. Keep frozen eval rows and prompt
  signatures out of training.
- Add a versioned continuous-eval matrix for DeepSeek V4 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna Mid via Codex,
  Gemma 4 E2B base, and the tuned Gemma 4 E2B GGUF. Use the same frozen prompt set and static
  scorer; keep Linux/GNU results separate from historical macOS/BSD baselines.
- Export the tuned adapter as a merged Gemma 4 E2B GGUF (target Q4_K_M) and verify a deterministic
  `llama.cpp` smoke inference with the exact Gemma 4 chat template before publishing it.

## Plan

1. Freeze and analyze the v1 base-vs-adapter artifact, turning regressions into a failure taxonomy.
2. Extend the source registry and collector with high-quality, license-compatible human-authored
   material for the weighted domains; deduplicate and manually review prompt/command pairs.
3. Build v2 SFT plus format-repair/hard-negative data with domain/language/source caps and a clean
   validation holdout.
4. Add provider adapters and a versioned result schema for the four continuous-eval targets without
   executing generated commands by default.
5. Retrain only after dataset gates pass; require positive paired strict-pass delta and no meaningful
   EN/KO regression before promotion.
6. Merge/export Q4_K_M GGUF, run `llama.cpp` smoke inference, record hashes/tool versions, and keep
   the adapter if GGUF conversion or parity verification fails.

## Done when

- Source lock, licenses, weighted domain counts, language counts, and contamination checks are
  reproducible.
- All four targets produce comparable frozen-suite reports under one protocol/version.
- The tuned checkpoint beats the Gemma 4 E2B base on paired strict pass without a material language
  regression.
- Adapter and Q4_K_M GGUF artifacts have SHA-256 hashes and the GGUF passes deterministic
  `llama.cpp` JSON-output smoke inference.
- No generated command is executed outside the explicit isolated container oracle.

title: Feature Request: Built-in Policies for Spend Limits, Service Allowlists, and Time Windows
content:
## Summary

Extend the existing hooks-and-policies system with a set of first-class, ready-to-use policy implementations covering the most common agentic guardrails: per-transaction spend caps, daily budgets, recipient allowlists, and time windows. Today consumers must implement `BasePolicy` themselves; these should ship with the kit.

## Motivation

Based on AI Bounty Feedback: #933 #931

The current kit ships two built-in policies (`MaxRecipientsPolicy`, `RejectToolPolicy`). Developers building payment-focused agents still need to implement spending limits and recipient restrictions manually — duplicating work across projects and increasing the surface area for mistakes in security-critical code.

Community interest confirms the gap: a working demo was built independently at https://github.com/s97472091-pixel/hedera-policy-agent as part of Hedera AI Bounty Week 5.

## Proposed Policies

### 1. `MaxTransferPolicy`

Blocks any single tool execution that would transfer more than a configured HBAR amount.

```ts
new MaxTransferPolicy(100) // reject any single transfer > 100 HBAR
```

- Enforced at `post-parameter-normalization` — before the transaction is built.
- Applies to HBAR transfers; HTS token amounts are checked against a configurable HBAR-equivalent rate.

### 2. `DailyLimitPolicy`

Caps total outgoing spend within a rolling 24-hour window.

```ts
new DailyLimitPolicy(500) // max 500 HBAR cumulative per day
```

- Tracks cumulative spend across `post-core-action` calls.
- State is in-memory by default; accepts an optional persistence adapter for multi-instance deployments.
- Exposes `getStats()` returning `{ spent, remaining, windowResetsAt }` for observability.

### 3. `RecipientAllowlistPolicy`

Rejects transfers to any account not on an explicit allowlist.

```ts
new RecipientAllowlistPolicy(['0.0.12345', '0.0.67890'])
```

- Enforced at `pre-tool-execution` — no transaction is ever built for a blocked recipient.
- Supports wildcard patterns (`0.0.*`) for shard/realm flexibility.
- `mode: 'audit'` logs violations without blocking, for gradual rollout.

### 4. `TimeWindowPolicy`

Allows tool execution only within configured time ranges.

```ts
new TimeWindowPolicy({
  allowedDays: ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'],
  allowedHours: { start: 9, end: 17 }, // 09:00–17:00 UTC
  timezone: 'UTC',
})
```

- Blocked at `pre-tool-execution`.
- Multiple windows compose via `TimeWindowPolicy.any([...windows])`.

## End-to-End Example

```ts
import {
  MaxTransferPolicy,
  DailyLimitPolicy,
  RecipientAllowlistPolicy,
  TimeWindowPolicy,
} from '@hedera-agent-kit/core';

const policies = [
  new MaxTransferPolicy(100),                        // max 100 HBAR per tx
  new DailyLimitPolicy(500),                         // max 500 HBAR per day
  new RecipientAllowlistPolicy(['0.0.12345']),        // approved recipients only
  new TimeWindowPolicy({                             // business hours only
    allowedDays: ['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'],
    allowedHours: { start: 9, end: 17 },
  }),
];

const toolkit = new HederaLangchainToolkit({
  client,
  configuration: {
    plugins: allCorePlugins,
    context: { mode: AgentMode.AUTONOMOUS, policies },
  },
});
```

## API Surface

All policies implement the existing `BasePolicy` interface — no core lifecycle changes are needed. They are exported from the main package entry point:

```ts
import {
  MaxTransferPolicy,
  DailyLimitPolicy,
  RecipientAllowlistPolicy,
  TimeWindowPolicy,
} from '@hedera-agent-kit/core';
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Each policy ships with unit tests covering allow, reject, and boundary-value scenarios.
- [ ] Each policy is documented in `docs/HOOKS_AND_POLICIES.md` under "Available Policies".
- [ ] Policies compose cleanly — multiple instances can be passed in the `policies` array without conflict.
- [ ] `DailyLimitPolicy` exposes `getStats()` for current window spend.
- [ ] `RecipientAllowlistPolicy` supports `mode: 'audit'` for non-blocking observation.

title: Support per-tool strict schema passthrough in defineTool
content:
### What problem are you trying to solve?

The AI SDK supports a per-tool `strict?: boolean` flag for function tools, and OpenAI-compatible providers can forward it as `tools[].function.strict`. Eve currently has no public or compiled representation for that flag:

- `ToolDefinition` / `PublicToolDefinition` do not expose `strict`.
- `InternalToolDefinition` and `CompiledToolDefinition` do not carry it.
- The compiled manifest schema has no `strict` field for tools.

As a result, an authored Eve tool cannot opt into provider-native strict tool calling. Adding `strict: true` behind a cast is not sufficient because the compiler/runtime boundary does not preserve the field.

Minimal API shape that is currently unavailable:

```ts
import { defineTool } from "eve/tools";
import { z } from "zod";

export default defineTool({
  description: "Get weather for a city.",
  inputSchema: z.object({ city: z.string() }),
  strict: true,
  execute({ city }) {
    return { city, temperatureC: 24 };
  },
});
```

This matters for providers that offer schema-constrained function calling. DeepSeek's strict tool mode, for example, requires `strict: true` on every function in the request and validates all submitted JSON Schemas before generation:

https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/tool_calls/

Without an Eve-level pass-through, applications must maintain a patch/fork, bypass Eve's harness, or give up provider-guaranteed argument conformance. This also needs to cover Eve framework tools: a provider that requires every function to be strict cannot be supported by forwarding the field only for authored tools.

This is separate from #542. That proposal makes invalid tool calls observable; this request allows providers to prevent schema-invalid arguments during generation.

Observed on `eve@0.22.4`; I also inspected the published `eve@0.22.6` types and manifest schema and did not find a strict-tool field.

### Proposed solution

Add an optional, default-off `strict?: boolean` field to Eve's tool definition pipeline and preserve it unchanged through compilation and runtime assembly.

Suggested scope:

1. Add `strict?: boolean` to the public and shared tool definition types.
2. Add it to `InternalToolDefinition`, `CompiledToolDefinition`, and the compiled manifest schema/version handling.
3. Preserve it for static authored tools, dynamic tools, extension tools, subagent tools, and authored replacements of framework tools.
4. Forward it when Eve constructs the AI SDK function tool passed to the model.
5. Keep `undefined` as the default so existing agents and providers are unchanged.
6. Optionally expose the resolved value from `eve info` for debugging.

Suggested tests:

- `defineTool({ strict: true })` type-checks.
- `true`, `false`, and `undefined` survive compile-manifest-runtime round trips.
- The final AI SDK tool received by a mock language model contains the expected flag.
- Static and dynamic authored tools behave consistently.
- Existing tools with no `strict` field produce unchanged requests.

I would keep provider capability detection and schema rewriting out of this first change. Eve should faithfully carry the author's intent; the provider can reject unsupported strict schemas, and applications can add provider-specific schema linting before enabling the flag.

### Alternatives considered

- **Local patch/fork of Eve:** feasible, but every Eve upgrade must rebase and revalidate the compiler/runtime patch.
- **Cast `strict: true` through `any`:** does not solve the compiled manifest and runtime propagation gap.
- **Call the AI SDK directly outside Eve:** loses Eve's durable sessions, event stream, approvals, tools, and eval harness for that model call.
- **Rewrite application schemas without changing Eve:** useful preparation, but it still cannot put `strict: true` on the provider request.
- **A provider-global strict option:** less precise and does not match the AI SDK's current per-tool contract; it also makes mixed-provider agents harder to support safely.

title: v1.0 — Persistent Vector Index Substrate (vectorlite) — deferred from #1005
content:
# v1.0 — Persistent Vector Index Substrate (vectorlite) — DEFERRED from #1005

**Origin:** carved out of #1005 by the v0.9.0 design vote of 2026-07-01 (15-agent codegraph-grounded review + 2×5 vote; tally 7 MODIFY / 3 ACCEPT / 0 DEFER, 10/10 `v090_fit=true` for the carve-down). Operator-confirmed decision: v0.9.0 ships only a minimal inert opt-in slice (tracked in #1005, rewritten); the full substrate re-platforming below is v1.0 scope.

## Deferred to this issue (v1.0)

- vectorlite / any SQLite loadable-extension backend + `build.rs` native `.so`/`.dylib`/`.dll` acquisition. Blockers found: rusqlite 0.32 is `bundled` with `load_extension` OFF; extension availability breaks the 3-OS (Windows-required) CI matrix, 5 release channels, and reproducible builds.
- u64 re-keying of vector ids (live model is String cids).
- Signed `IndexInserted`/`IndexDeleted` events on the default write path (anti-idiom on-by-default; if pulled earlier it must be an opt-in additive `event_type` on `SignedEvent`, net-delta verify only, no caller `prev_hash`).
- Builtin persistent WAL backend — flagged RISK #1 in review: cross-domain 2PC hazard; as-written the fallback for high-assurance environments would get the WEAKER coherence guarantee.
- One-shot migration + rebuild primitive (original Tasks 3.1/3.2).
- rabitq-rs alternate backend.
- The 15-agent fan-out execution model (merge-order coupled; mislabelled parallel).

## Blocking gates carried forward

- Task 0.1 recall spike stays strictly blocking (standalone /tmp binary; R@5 within 1.0pt of the 97.8% baseline).
- NEW co-equal blocking pre-flight: the pinned extension must load + smoke-query on macOS AND Windows CI runners before any substrate work fans out — extension availability across the matrix/channels is the real plan-killer, not R@5.
- p95 ≤ 35ms is advisory only (no macOS bench runner exists).

## ⚠️ Stale-anchor warning on the original plan below

The plan was drafted against a stale tree and MUST be re-grounded before execution:
- Proposes a `VectorIndex` **trait** — the name collides with the concrete struct at `src/hnsw.rs` (23+ callers). v0.9 introduces the seam as `VectorSearchIndex` instead.
- References phantom symbols: `src/recall/mod.rs::filter_by_namespace_post_ann` (Task 2.3), a `MemoryStore` HNSW field (`MemoryStore` is a trait at `src/store/mod.rs`), `src/audit/signed_events.rs` (wrong path).
- Assumes u64 ids (live: String cids) and `&mut self` + `rusqlite::Transaction` (live: deliberate `&self` + interior-Mutex + `Arc<Mutex<Option<VectorIndex>>>` swap-on-read).
- Assumes schema v34; CURRENT_SCHEMA_VERSION was already 74+ at review time.

Smaller drops are acceptable but must be documented honestly in the v0.9 release notes per the project's audit-honesty discipline. Output structured JSON at `benchmarks/results/longmemeval_v0.9_<variant>.json` for each variant. Regenerate the recall comparison chart at `docs/recall_v0.9.svg`. Update `benchmarks/longmemeval/README.md` with the new numbers and a one-paragraph honest summary of any regressions.

**Gate criteria:** Default-config R@5 within 0.5 points of baseline, all six variants reported, charts regenerated.

### Task 4.4 — PERFORMANCE.md baselines + bench CI guard

**Owner:** Agent M.
**Duration estimate:** ~1 hour.
**Depends on:** All merges complete.

**Starter prompt:**

> You are Agent M. Update `PERFORMANCE.md` with v0.9 baselines for both vectorlite and builtin backends on the M2 reference hardware. The relevant budgets that may shift: `memory_store` keyword/semantic/autonomous (insert-time impact of writing the new index event), `memory_recall` semantic/autonomous (the structural change from post-filter to pre-filter), `memory_search` keyword (unchanged but verify). Add new budgets for new operations: `memory_reindex` per-1000-memories (LLM-bound, document the expected range), `migration` per-1000-memories (one-shot, document expected wall time). Run `cargo bench --bench v0_9_index_budgets` to populate. Update `performance/baseline.json` with the new numbers. The CI guard at `.github/workflows/bench.yml` already fails PRs that exceed budget by >10% — verify it still triggers correctly on a synthetic 15%-regression test. Document in `PERFORMANCE.md` the expected difference between vectorlite (faster, persistent) and builtin (slightly slower, more portable) so operators can make informed selection.

**Gate criteria:** baselines updated, CI guard verified, documentation clearly compares backends.

### Task 4.5 — ai-memory doctor integration + V08-PE-8 verifier extension

**Owner:** Agent N.
**Duration estimate:** ~1 hour.
**Depends on:** All merges complete.

**Starter prompt:**

> You are Agent N. Extend `ai-memory doctor` and the V08-PE-8 audit-trail verifier with the new v0.9 surface. Add to `ai-memory doctor`: an "index drift" check that counts rows in `memories`, counts vectors in the active backend, counts `IndexInserted` − `IndexDeleted` events in `signed_events`, and flags any mismatch. An "embedder dim violations" check that reports the `embedder_dim_violations_count` from the capabilities envelope. An "index backend" status line showing the active backend, whether fallback occurred at boot, and persistence mode. A "rebuild status" section showing any in-progress reindex operation with progress and ETA. Extend `ai-memory verify-audit-trail` to walk the new `IndexInserted | IndexDeleted | IndexRebuilt | IndexMigrationCompleted` event types: verify Ed25519 signatures, verify prev_hash chain continuity across the boundary between memory events and index events, verify that for every `IndexInserted` there exists a corresponding `memories` row, verify that for every `IndexDeleted` the memory_id is absent from the active index (call the trait's verify(id) method). Add a test that injects a mismatch (delete a vector from the index without emitting the signed event) and confirms the verifier catches it. Update `docs/security/audit-trail-coverage.md` with the new event kinds.

**Gate criteria:** doctor reports all new fields correctly, verifier catches injected mismatches, audit-trail-coverage doc reflects new event surface.

### Task 4.6 — release notes, CHANGELOG, capabilities envelope v3 doc

**Owner:** Agent O.
**Duration estimate:** ~1 hour.
**Depends on:** All merges complete; ideally also after Agents J–N have reported so release notes can honestly state results.

**Starter prompt:**

> You are Agent O. Write the v0.9 release notes at `docs/v0.9.0/release-notes.md` and update `CHANGELOG.md`. The release notes structure follows v0.7.0's: executive summary in three sentences, the audit-gap-closures section (G2, G3, G4, §5.2 post-ANN filter), the new capabilities section (vectorlite + builtin backends, rebuild primitive, embedder-version tracking, signed index events), the migration section (how operators upgrade, what they'll see, rollback path), the cutline section (anything that slipped from this scope), the honest disclosures section (any recall regressions from Agent L's report, any performance shifts from Agent M's report, any new dependencies). Update `CHANGELOG.md` with the standard ai-memory format. Update `docs/capabilities-v3.md` with the full v3 envelope schema including all v0.9 additions. Update `ROADMAP2.md` to mark §5.4 G2, G3, G4 as SHIPPED with the v0.9.0 reference, and to mark the §5.2 post-ANN filter hazard as RESOLVED. The release notes must follow the project's honesty discipline — do not paper over any regressions Agents J–N reported. If LongMemEval R@5 dropped by 0.3 points on builtin backend, say so explicitly. Cross-link to the structured JSON benchmark results so readers can verify independently.

**Gate criteria:** Release notes are honest about regressions, CHANGELOG follows project format, ROADMAP2.md correctly updated, capabilities-v3.md complete.

---

## 5. Release

### Task 5.1 — tag, sign, push to all 5 channels

**Owner:** Agent P (release agent).
**Duration estimate:** ~30 minutes if all channels are healthy.
**Depends on:** All 4.x verification tasks green.

**Starter prompt:**

> You are Agent P. v0.9.0 is ready to cut. Verify all of these are green before tagging: ship-gate 4/4 on both backends, A2A-gate ironclaw-mtls 48/48 on both backends, LongMemEval default-config R@5 within 0.5 of baseline, PERFORMANCE.md baselines updated and CI guard passing, doctor + verifier integration complete, release notes honest. If any of these is red, refuse to cut and escalate. If all green: GPG-sign the tag `v0.9.0` against the operator key, push to GitHub, and trigger the release pipeline that publishes to crates.io, Homebrew tap, Fedora COPR, Docker GHCR, APT PPA. After each channel publishes, run the smoke test (`memory_capabilities` returns valid v3 envelope showing `index_backend` populated correctly). If any channel smoke test fails, file `v0.9-distribution-blocker` with the channel name and the failure mode but do not roll back the tag — the standard procedure is to ship a v0.9.0.1 patch through the failing channel. Update the public landing pages (ship-gate, A2A-gate) by posting the new result JSON to the auto-update endpoint. Post a release announcement to the project's standard channels following the v0.7.0 template.

**Gate criteria:** Tag exists, signed, all 5 channels publish, smoke tests pass, landing pages updated.

---

## 6. Critical-path timing summary

```
Hour 0.0–0.75 ┃ Task 0.1 spike (BLOCKING, single agent)
              ┃   ├─ Gate: vectorlite recall holds
              ┃   └─ If fail: re-plan with rabitq-rs as primary
Hour 0.75–1.0 ┃ Task 1.1 trait stub (single agent)
              ┃   └─ Trait stub pushed at minute 30 of 1.1
Hour 1.0–4.0  ┃ PARALLEL FAN-OUT (9 agents on 9 tasks)
              ┃   ├─ Agent A: 1.1 (continues, full impl)
              ┃   ├─ Agent B: 1.2 vectorlite backend (3h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent C: 1.3 builtin backend (2h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent D: 1.4 factory + capabilities (1h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent E: 2.1 signed events (2h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent F: 2.2 dim enforcement (1.5h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent G: 2.3 namespace prefilter (2h, after B tags)
              ┃   ├─ Agent H: 3.1 migration (2h)
              ┃   └─ Agent I: 3.2 rebuild primitive (3h, after F tags)
Hour 4.0–5.5  ┃ INTEGRATION (single coordinator + fix agents)
              ┃   └─ Merge order: A → C → B → D → F → E → G → H → I
Hour 5.5–7.0  ┃ PARALLEL VERIFICATION (6 agents)
              ┃   ├─ Agent J: 4.1 ship-gate (1.5h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent K: 4.2 A2A-gate (1h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent L: 4.3 LongMemEval (1h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent M: 4.4 PERFORMANCE.md (1h)
              ┃   ├─ Agent N: 4.5 doctor + verifier (1h)
              ┃   └─ Agent O: 4.6 release notes (1h, blocks on J-N partial)
Hour 7.0–7.5  ┃ Task 5.1 release (single agent)
              ┃   └─ Five channels published, smoke-tested, landing pages updated
```

**Floor:** 4 hours if no surprises and the spike clears in 20 minutes.
**Expected:** 7 hours with normal integration friction (1–2 fix cycles).
**Ceiling:** 10 hours if a recall regression triggers a backend swap (re-plan against rabitq-rs).

---

## 7. Risk register

**Recall regression at the spike (Task 0.1).** Mitigation: pre-planned re-run against rabitq-rs as primary, same trait, same hour count. Decision belongs to the operator, not the spike agent.

**vectorlite extension loading blocked in target environment.** Mitigation: Agent D's factory falls back to builtin transparently. End user sees a structured warning, not a daemon failure.

**Windows ARM64 vectorlite untested.** Mitigation: Agent J's ship-gate runs on Windows ARM64 CI runner if available; if not, document the gap and ship builtin as default on Windows ARM64 for one release cycle while CI catches up.

**Migration interrupted on a 10M+ memory database.** Mitigation: Agent H's idempotent restartable design. The state table tracks last completed memory_id; resumption is automatic on next start.

**Audit chain hash mismatch under concurrent write load.** Mitigation: Agent E's signing emitter is sequenced through a single tokio task with bounded mpsc channel — no parallel signing, no chain race. This is correct-but-not-maximally-parallel; if throughput becomes the binding constraint later, a Merkle batching strategy can be added behind the same interface.

**Build-time download of vectorlite extension binary fails.** Mitigation: pin the GitHub release artifact hash, fail the build loudly if SHA mismatch, document the offline-build path using a vendored binary in `vendor/vectorlite/`.

---

## 8. Out of scope for v0.9 (explicitly deferred)

- **Quantization backends.** RaBitQ-IVF, TurboQuant, residual VQ — all pluggable via the trait but not shipped in v0.9. Belongs in v0.10 or later when corpus size demands it.
- **GPU acceleration.** Not a substrate concern. Commercial-tier deployment may add this behind the same trait.
- **Per-namespace HNSW shards.** Mentioned in ROADMAP2.md §5.4 G2 fallback; the namespace pre-filter solution (Task 2.3) addresses the same hazard more cleanly. Revisit if filter selectivity becomes a measured problem.
- **Asymmetric distance computation** (compressed corpus, full-precision query). Quantization-era concern. Defer.
- **Streaming consistency under data-dependent quantization** (December 2025 paper). Research direction; not yet a production primitive.

---

## 9. Definition of done

v0.9 ships when all of these hold simultaneously:

1. Tasks 0.1, 1.1–1.4, 2.1–2.3, 3.1–3.2, 4.1–4.6, 5.1 have closed against their gate criteria.
2. ROADMAP2.md §5.4 G2, G3, G4 are marked SHIPPED with v0.9.0 references.
3. ROADMAP2.md §5.2 "post-ANN namespace filter production hazard" is marked RESOLVED with v0.9.0 reference.
4. The VectorIndex trait is documented, the two backends ship, the factory selects correctly under all flag combinations.
5. The release notes honestly disclose any regressions found by Agents J–N.
6. Five distribution channels publish v0.9.0 with passing smoke tests.
7. Public landing pages (ship-gate, A2A-gate) reflect v0.9.0 results.

---

title: Is COL_LENGTH sufficient for parameter sanitation
content:
I have a stored procedure that we are scanning using some AI tools to look for vulnerabilities. I am doing a dynamic SQL statement with an order by clause and that parameter for that order by I am running through this within a :

Later I build dynamic SQL using 

The AI tool says this can be exploited and I just don't think so.

SQL injection: The stored procedure constructs dynamic SQL by concatenating user-provided parameters like @OrderByColumn and @OrderByType directly into the query string. While there is validation using COL_LENGTH, this approach is inherently risky. An attacker could potentially bypass the validation or exploit edge cases to inject malicious SQL code. The safer approach would be to use a whitelist of allowed column names and directions, or use parameterized queries with proper escaping.
